title: She Insisted She Belonged to No Movement. Somebody Filed Her Under Minimalism Anyway.
standfirst: Mira Schendel was baptised Catholic, classified as Jewish under Mussolini's racial laws, and reached São Paulo alone in 1953 after a decade of exile across three countries. She spent the next three decades building a practice out of what language does and doesn't show — which makes the one-word label attached to this sheet almost exactly backwards.

sections.heading: A Label for a Movement She Said She Never Joined
sections.body: Minimalism, in the sense the twentieth century actually used the word, was an argument for objects that refuse to mean anything beyond their own surface — Judd's boxes, LeWitt's grids, structures built to stop a viewer looking for content. Schendel's late work is built from almost nothing but content: rice paper crowded with handwriting in Italian, German, Portuguese and French, pressed under acrylic so the words drift and overlap rather than settle. Her own [Wikipedia entry states plainly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mira_Schendel) that she had no ties to any specific school or movement, and she resisted the Brazilian labels critics tried to fix her under just as hard. Of a closely related series she said only that she wanted [to show that the back of transparency](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v35/n20/anne-wagner/at-tate-modern) lies in front of you — a sentence built to resist exactly the kind of one-word classification a database needs in order to function.

sections.heading: A Catholic Baptism Did Not Save Her From the Racial Laws
sections.body: She was born Myrrha Dagmar Dub in Zurich in 1919, the daughter of a Jewish fabric merchant and a milliner who had her [baptised Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mira_Schendel) within the year. The family later settled in Milan, where she grew up practising Catholic and studying philosophy at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore. None of it mattered in 1938: Mussolini's racial laws classified her as Jewish through her father's line, stripped her Italian citizenship, and ended her university studies. She left Italy in 1939, crossing Switzerland and Austria before joining a stream of refugees into Sarajevo, where she spent the war and married her first husband, Josep Hargesheimer, in 1941. The couple returned to Italy afterwards on displaced-persons' papers; Schendel worked for the International Refugee Organization in Rome before they emigrated to Brazil in August 1949, settling first in Porto Alegre. They separated in 1953, and she went on alone to São Paulo.

sections.heading: A Physicist Handed Her a Box of Rice Paper
sections.body: In São Paulo she fell in with a circle of émigré intellectuals that included the physicist and critic Mário Schenberg and the philosopher Vilém Flusser, another Central European rebuilding a career from nothing. It was Schenberg who gave her rice paper in the early 1960s. Between 1964 and 1966 she turned it into roughly 2,000 monotype drawings: paint applied to a glass plate, dusted with talcum powder, then a sheet of paper laid on top and worked with her fingernails and a stylus, so the marks read as though they were surfacing from inside the paper rather than sitting on it. Her friendship with Flusser ran alongside the discovery for two decades, conducted largely in argument on the terrace of his São Paulo flat, about language, kitsch, and what it meant to see through something without emptying it of meaning. He later wrote about her at length in his own memoir, crediting the relationship with reshaping his thinking about art as much as he had sharpened her practice.

sections.heading: Language as Material, Not Caption
sections.body: By the 1968 Venice Biennale she was showing what she called graphic objects: rice paper overwritten with handwritten letters and near-letters, pressed between plexiglass panels so the words hovered rather than sat on a page. One, made in response to Stockhausen's *Song of the Youths*, [repeated a single word across six languages](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v35/n20/anne-wagner/at-tate-modern) — FEUER fuoco fire FEU feuer FUOCO — the repetition doing the work a translation would normally hide. The notebook sheets she made in 1970 and 1971, [Letraset lettering and hand-drawn geometric lines encased in Plexiglas](https://www.phillips.com/detail/mira-schendel/NY010513/27), carry the same logic further. That interest in language as a physical thing rather than a clear window onto meaning has been traced partly to her background — [a Jewish family's traditional wariness of images](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/tate-papers/21/mira-schendels-gesture-on-art-in-vilem-flussers-thought-with-mira-schendel-by-flusser), inherited underneath a Catholic upbringing that formally forbade her none of it. In 1968 she also travelled to Switzerland to visit the philosopher Jean Gebser, whose [religious model of transparency](https://www.flusserstudies.net/archive/flusser-studies-19-may-2015-special-italian-issue) — seeing through something as a spiritual act, not just an optical one — she adopted afterward to describe her own work.

sections.heading: Respected at Home, Unknown Abroad, Then Priced Like Neither
sections.body: Schendel worked in São Paulo for thirty-five years and died there of lung cancer in 1988, respected inside Brazil as one of the country's defining modernists and barely known outside it. That changed in September 2013, when [Tate Modern opened the first full international retrospective](https://www.tate.org.uk/press/press-releases/mira-schendel-1) of her career — more than 270 paintings, drawings and sculptures, many shown for the first time anywhere. The market followed the scholarship. In 1965 she had built a series of knotted rice-paper sculptures, the Droguinhas, explicitly, in her own words, [in open opposition to the 'permanent' and 'ownable'](https://awarewomenartists.com/en/magazine/tout-ou-rien-les-droguinhas-de-mira-schendel/); keeping one intact, she said, was like keeping the artist David Medalla's foam sculptures, since whoever owns a thing like that won't let it simply be. In May 2017, one of those objects went to auction at [Sotheby's in New York, estimated at $1.2 to $1.8 million](https://www.sothebys.com/en/auctions/ecatalogue/2017/contemporary-art-evening-auction-n09761/lot.40.html).
